source: FDA label of Depakote (divalproex sodium) through openFDA
quote: A significantly higher proportion of valproate patients had somnolence compared to placebo, and although not statistically significant, there was a higher proportion of patients with dehydration. [...] There was a trend for the patients who experienced these events to have a lower baseline albumin concentration, lower valproate clearance, and a higher BUN.
second_mechanism_or_limit: A trend in one trial of elderly patients with dementia; lower clearance and a higher urea nitrogen went with the lower albumin, so the carrier is one of three candidates.

source: Madan et al. 2021, Br J Clin Pharmacol, abstract in PubMed
quote: For the valproate cohort, hypoalbuminaemia (42% vs. 28%, P = .039) and albumin-adjusted valproate concentration >100 mg L(49% vs. 23%, P < .001) were both associated with increased neurotoxicity.
second_mechanism_or_limit: One hospital, retrospective, 383 patients; the abstract does not break neurotoxicity down by symptom, so the check reads the drug's own kept positive symptoms.

source: Doré et al. 2017, Pharmacotherapy, abstract in PubMed
quote: This study showed that in the presence of hypoalbuminemia, high unbound VPA concentrations can be observed despite normal or low total VPA concentrations. It also demonstrated that high unbound VPA concentrations are associated with clinically significant neurologic adverse symptoms.
second_mechanism_or_limit: 41 patients, retrospective. The abstract names 'saturable protein binding and saturable metabolism' as the reason total concentrations mislead for valproate; a drug without them need not behave so.

source: FDA label of Phenytoin Sodium Injection through openFDA
quote: Because the fraction of unbound phenytoin is increased in patients with renal or hepatic disease, or in those with hypoalbuminemia, the monitoring of phenytoin serum levels should be based on the unbound fraction in those patients.
second_mechanism_or_limit: States a higher unbound fraction and a monitoring instruction, no symptom. The guideline of the International League Against Epilepsy states the expectation the other way: 'Although unbound drug concentrations will not be affected by changes in serum proteins, changes in protein binding need to be taken into account when interpreting total serum drug concentrations' (Patsalos et al. 2008, doi:10.1111/j.1528-1167.2008.01561.x).

source: Madan et al. 2021, Br J Clin Pharmacol, abstract in PubMed
quote: On logistic regression, higher albumin-adjusted phenytoin concentration was an independent risk factor for neurotoxicity (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.01-1.12, P = .011).
second_mechanism_or_limit: The association is with the albumin-adjusted concentration, which stands in for the unbound concentration; the abstract reports no association of hypoalbuminaemia itself with neurotoxicity for phenytoin. 144 patients, one hospital.

source: FDA label of Depakote (divalproex sodium) through openFDA
quote: Valproate displaces phenytoin from its plasma albumin binding sites and inhibits its hepatic metabolism. Co-administration of valproate (400 mg TID) with phenytoin (250 mg) in normal volunteers (n=7) was associated with a 60% increase in the free fraction of phenytoin.
second_mechanism_or_limit: Second mechanism in the same sentence: inhibition of metabolism. Lai and Huang 1993 (doi:10.1002/bdd.2510140409, abstract in PubMed) attribute the rise in unbound phenytoin to it: 'the enzyme inhibition by valproic acid increased both the total and unbound concentration of phenytoin'.

source: FDA label of Depakote (divalproex sodium) through openFDA
quote: Valproate displaces diazepam from its plasma albumin binding sites and inhibits its metabolism. Co-administration of valproate (1,500 mg daily) increased the free fraction of diazepam (10 mg) by 90% in healthy volunteers (n=6).
second_mechanism_or_limit: Second mechanism in the same sentence: inhibition of metabolism. Six volunteers.

source: FDA label of Depakote (divalproex sodium) through openFDA
quote: Conversely, valproate may displace certain protein-bound drugs (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, and tolbutamide)
second_mechanism_or_limit: No measurement for carbamazepine in the label. Its interaction paragraph reports a change in metabolism: 'Serum levels of carbamazepine (CBZ) decreased 17% while that of carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide (CBZ-E) increased by 45% upon co-administration of valproate and CBZ to epileptic patients.'

source: FDA label of Depakote (divalproex sodium) through openFDA
quote: A study involving the co-administration of aspirin at antipyretic doses (11 to 16 mg/kg) with valproate to pediatric patients (n=6) revealed a decrease in protein binding and an inhibition of metabolism of valproate. Valproate free fraction was increased 4-fold in the presence of aspirin compared to valproate alone.
second_mechanism_or_limit: Second mechanism in the same sentence: inhibition of metabolism. Six children.

source: Patsalos et al. 2008, Epilepsia, full text through Wiley Scholar Gateway
quote: Valproic acid, tolbutamide, aspirin, and some other nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs displace phenytoin from albumin binding sites [...] resulting in a decrease in total drug concentrations, while the unbound concentration remains unchanged or may even increase when the displacing drug also inhibits phenytoin metabolism.
second_mechanism_or_limit: The sentence itself says the unbound concentration stays unchanged unless metabolism is inhibited as well, so this statement supports displacement and not a larger effect.
